analogy.p: Imagine a lump of raisin dough rising in the oven. The raisins are galaxies and the dough is space. As the dough expands, every raisin moves away from every other raisin. Pick any raisin: its neighbours move away slowly, but raisins further away have more dough in between, which stretches more, so they move away faster. No raisin is at the centre; each sees the same pattern. The analogy breaks down because the dough has an edge and a centre and the raisins themselves are fixed in size, whereas the real universe has no edge or centre we can point to, and space is not 'inside' anything.

bullets: Observation: the light from distant galaxies has longer wavelengths than expected, so it is **red-shifted**.
Pattern: the further away the galaxy, the **greater the red-shift** and the **faster** it is moving away from us.
Interpretation: **space itself is expanding**, so galaxies are moving apart.
Big Bang model: the universe began from a **very small, extremely hot and dense** region and has been expanding since.
Second evidence: **CMB radiation**, a form of electromagnetic radiation filling the whole universe, which the Big Bang model predicts.
Always say WHY: each observation is only evidence because the Big Bang model explains it and other models struggle to.
core.h: What the specification asks you to know
core.p: This is a **physics-only** (triple science) part of the AQA Space physics topic. You must be able to explain that there is a **red-shift** in the light from almost all distant galaxies, that the **further away** a galaxy is the **faster** it is moving away and the **greater** its red-shift, and that these observations are evidence that the universe is **expanding**, which supports the **Big Bang** model. You also need to know what the Big Bang model says and be able to describe the **cosmic microwave background radiation (CMBR)** as a second piece of evidence. Questions are mostly explanations, so the aim is to learn the chain of reasoning in the right order.

bullets: Source moving **towards** the observer: wavelength **decreases**, frequency **increases** (higher pitch for sound, shifted towards the blue end for light).
Source moving **away** from the observer: wavelength **increases**, frequency **decreases** (lower pitch for sound, shifted towards the red end for light).

The **speed** of the wave does not change; it is set by the medium (for light, about 3.0 x 10^8 m/s in a vacuum). Since wave speed = frequency x wavelength, a longer wavelength means a lower frequency.
The effect happens for all waves, including sound and light, so it can be used on light from space.
Bigger relative speed means a bigger change in wavelength, which is why the size of the shift tells astronomers how fast a galaxy is moving.
Link to waves topic: use v = f x wavelength to explain why one goes up when the other goes down.
core.h: The Doppler effect: the idea behind red-shift
core.p: The **Doppler effect** is the change in the **observed frequency and wavelength** of a wave when the **source of the wave is moving relative to the observer**. You hear it when an ambulance siren passes you: the pitch is higher as it approaches and lower as it moves away. As the source moves towards you, each new wave crest is emitted from a position closer to you than the previous one, so crests arrive more often and the waves are squashed together. As it moves away, each crest starts further away, so crests arrive less often and are stretched out.

bullets: Atoms in the outer layers of stars absorb light at **specific wavelengths** that are a fingerprint of each element, producing dark lines in the star's spectrum.
The same pattern is measured in a laboratory on Earth, using for example hydrogen, so the **reference wavelengths** are known (the main hydrogen line is at about 656 nm).
In light from a distant galaxy the whole pattern is found at **longer wavelengths** than in the lab. Every line has moved the same way, which shows it is a genuine shift and not a different element.
The **larger the shift**, the faster the galaxy is moving away.
The colour of the galaxy does not need to look red. It is the **positions of the lines** that matter.
A shift to shorter wavelengths is a **blue-shift**; a few nearby galaxies, such as Andromeda, show this because they are moving towards us (an extension fact).
core.h: Red-shift: what it is and how it is observed
core.p: **Red-shift** is the increase in the observed wavelength of light from a source that is moving away from us. It is called red-shift because visible light at the red end of the spectrum has the longest wavelength (about 700 nm) and violet the shortest (about 400 nm), so an increase in wavelength moves features **towards the red end** of the spectrum. Astronomers do not look for galaxies turning red; they use a **spectrometer** to split the light and look at the pattern of **dark absorption lines**.

bullets: Red-shift is measured directly from the light, so it is the observation. The **speed** is worked out from the size of the shift.
Distance and red-shift are positively correlated: plotted as a graph, distance against speed gives a line that slopes upwards and passes through the origin.
Do not describe the pattern as 'the further away, the less the red-shift'. This is the most common slip.
Distances to galaxies are measured by other methods, so the pattern is a result from combining two sets of measurements.
Light takes time to travel: when we see a distant galaxy we see it as it was **millions or billions of years ago**.
A **light-year** is the distance light travels in one year (about 9.5 x 10^12 km); it is a unit of distance, not of time.
core.p: When light from many galaxies was measured, two things were found. First, **almost all** the galaxies (apart from a few very close ones) show red-shift, so they are all moving **away from us**. Second, the **further away** a galaxy is, the **greater** its red-shift. A greater red-shift means a greater speed of recession, so the more distant galaxies are moving away **faster**. The speed is roughly **proportional** to the distance, so a galaxy twice as far away recedes about twice as fast.

bullets: The galaxies are not flying through space like fragments from an explosion; the **space between them is stretching**.
There is **no centre** of the expansion and no edge you can point to. Every observer sees the other galaxies move away from them.
Doubling the stretching doubles every distance: a galaxy 100 units away gains 100, one 200 units away gains 200. More distance gained in the same time is a greater speed.
The wavelength of light stretches too as it travels through expanding space, which is another way to think about red-shift.
Groups of galaxies held together by gravity (like our own Local Group) do not expand; the expansion is seen between distant clusters.
Link to the **analogy** below to picture this.
core.p: The observation that everything is moving away from us, with the most distant moving fastest, does **not** mean that we are at the centre of the universe. It is what you would see from **any** galaxy if **space itself is expanding**. As space stretches, the distance between any two galaxies grows, and a pair that start further apart gain more distance in the same time, so they separate faster. That is exactly the pattern seen.

bullets: The Big Bang was an **expansion of space itself**, not an explosion in one place in a space that already existed.
At the start the universe was incredibly **hot and dense**; as it expanded it **cooled**.
The age of the universe is about 13.8 billion years (a rounded value is fine in the exam).
It is a **scientific model** supported by evidence, so use the phrases 'evidence for' and 'supports' rather than 'proves'.
The model explains why all the galaxies are moving apart and also predicts the leftover radiation known as the CMB.
Stars, galaxies and planets formed later, after the universe had expanded and cooled (link to the life cycle of stars topic).
core.p: If the universe is expanding now, then in the past everything must have been **closer together**. Running the expansion backwards, all the matter and space of the universe were once in a **very small region** that was **extremely hot and dense**. The **Big Bang model** states that the universe began from this tiny region about **13.8 billion years ago** in a huge expansion, and that space has been expanding and cooling ever since. As it cooled, matter clumped under gravity to form stars and galaxies.

bullets: It was discovered accidentally in 1964 as unexplained background noise in a radio antenna (Penzias and Wilson), after the Big Bang model had predicted it.
It fills the **whole universe** and comes from all directions, so it is not from any one star or galaxy.
Today it corresponds to a very low temperature of about 2.7 K, which is about -270 degrees C.
Because the Big Bang model predicts it and other models struggle to, it is strong evidence for the Big Bang.
Two pieces of evidence make the case stronger than one: **red-shift** and **CMB radiation**.
Exam phrase: 'CMB radiation is the leftover radiation from the early hot universe, stretched to microwave wavelengths as the universe expanded'.
core.p: The **cosmic microwave background (CMB) radiation** is electromagnetic radiation, in the **microwave** region, that arrives from **every direction** in space with almost the same intensity. The Big Bang model explains it as **leftover radiation** from the very hot early universe. At first this radiation had a very short wavelength because the universe was so hot, but as space expanded the radiation was **stretched to much longer wavelengths**, now microwaves. This is red-shift on the grandest scale.

bullets: Evidence 1: red-shift of galaxies, with larger red-shift for more distant galaxies.
Evidence 2: the CMB radiation, found in every direction.
A theory is accepted when many independent pieces of evidence support it and it survives testing; it can still be improved if new evidence appears.
The Steady State theory is useful for 'compare theories' questions; you do not need more detail than 'it cannot explain the CMB'.
New observations (see the dark matter and dark energy note) are refining the model rather than overturning it.
Peer review and repeated measurements by different teams make the evidence reliable.
core.h: Why scientists accept the Big Bang model
core.p: A good model must **explain existing observations** and **make predictions that can be tested**. The Big Bang model explains the red-shift of galaxies and the pattern with distance, and it predicted a background radiation that was later found. An alternative idea, the **Steady State** theory, said the universe has always looked the same, with new matter created as it expands. It could explain red-shift but had **no explanation for the CMB**, so it lost support. This is how science works: models compete, and evidence decides.

bullets: We can only observe light, so we cannot directly 'see' the Big Bang itself; the earliest light we can detect is the CMB.
We see things as they were in the past because light takes a long time to arrive.
The model is a simplification of a very complicated process and is checked by more and more precise measurements.
It is wise to say 'supports' rather than 'proves' in explanation questions.
Different methods that agree on a result increase confidence that it is valid.
Models in science can be changed if new evidence does not fit.
core.h: Limits and cautions about the evidence
core.p: The measurements are made from Earth, using telescopes, so there are things to be careful about. Light from distant galaxies is very faint, the shifts must be measured very precisely, and distances to galaxies are hard to find, so there are **uncertainties**. This is why scientists look for several independent lines of evidence, and why examiners like answers that use the words 'evidence' and 'suggests'.

bullets: **Observation**: light from distant galaxies is red-shifted (wavelength increased, lines moved towards the red end).
**Pattern**: the further away the galaxy, the greater the red-shift, so the faster it is moving away.
**Interpretation**: galaxies are moving apart because space itself is expanding.
**Model**: working backwards, everything was once in a very small, hot, dense region, the Big Bang, about 13.8 billion years ago.
**Extra evidence**: CMB radiation is the leftover, stretched radiation from the hot early universe.
Finish with a **conclusion** word such as 'this supports the Big Bang model'.
core.h: Linking the ideas together: a model answer chain
core.p: Many marks are lost by writing the right facts in the wrong order. A reliable chain for a 4 or 6 mark answer is: **observation, pattern, interpretation, model, extra evidence**. Learn it as a single flowing argument so that you can deploy it whatever the question asks.

bullets: Waves: v = f x wavelength; visible spectrum 400 nm to 700 nm; microwaves have wavelengths of about millimetres to centimetres.
Electromagnetic spectrum: the CMB was once high-energy radiation and is now microwaves because its wavelength has been stretched.
Gravity: causes matter to clump into stars and galaxies after the Big Bang.
Stars: fusion in stars makes the heavier elements (life cycle of stars).
Scientific method: observation, hypothesis, prediction, testing, peer review, revised models.
Next topic: dark matter and dark energy extend the Big Bang model with new evidence (see that note).
core.h: Higher-order ideas and links to other topics
core.p: Space physics links to many other parts of physics. The wave equation and the electromagnetic spectrum give the maths and vocabulary of red-shift, gravity explains how galaxies and stars form, and nuclear fusion explains how stars shine. Linking these shows examiners that you understand the course as a connected whole, which is what top-grade answers do.

exam: Command words: **describe** = say what happens; **explain** = give reasons (use 'because', 'so', 'therefore'); **evaluate** = weigh strengths and weaknesses and give a judgement.
1 mark: a definition or a single fact, for example 'wavelength of light increases' or 'microwaves'.
2 marks: a statement plus a link, for example 'The further the galaxy, the greater the red-shift, so it is moving away faster'.
4 marks: the chain of observation, pattern, interpretation, model. Each link in the chain earns a mark, so do not skip one.
6 marks: include BOTH red-shift and CMB, explain why each supports the Big Bang, and finish with a conclusion. The best answers are in a logical order.
Use the exact phrases: 'wavelength of the light has increased', 'moved towards the red end of the spectrum', 'space itself is expanding', 'leftover radiation'.
If a table of wavelengths is given, work out the **shift** (observed minus lab wavelength) for each galaxy first; the largest shift is the fastest and, by the pattern, the furthest.
Graph questions: speed against distance is a straight line through the origin, so the speed is directly proportional to the distance.
Do not say that the galaxy 'changes colour'; talk about the wavelength of the light.

mistakes.r: Red-shift is an increase in the wavelength of the light, so the pattern of lines moves towards the red end of the spectrum. The galaxy need not look red.
mistakes.w: The galaxies are red-shifted because they look red.

mistakes.r: The further away the galaxy, the greater the red-shift and the faster it is moving away.
mistakes.w: The further away the galaxy, the smaller the red-shift.

mistakes.r: It was the expansion of space itself from a very small, hot, dense region. There is no centre.
mistakes.w: The Big Bang was an explosion in the middle of space.

mistakes.r: The speed of light does not change. The wavelength increases and the frequency decreases.
mistakes.w: The speed of light slows down so it looks red.

mistakes.r: Because space is expanding, observers in any galaxy would see the others move away. There is no centre.
mistakes.w: Everything moves away from us so we are at the centre of the universe.

mistakes.r: The CMB is leftover radiation from the early hot universe, stretched by expansion to microwave wavelengths, arriving from all directions.
mistakes.w: The CMB is light from a flash at the Big Bang that we can still see.

mistakes.r: Red-shift and CMB radiation are evidence that supports the Big Bang model. Use 'supports' or 'is evidence for'.
mistakes.w: Red-shift proves the Big Bang happened.

mistakes.r: Say that space itself is expanding, so the distance between galaxies increases.
mistakes.w: The galaxies are moving away because they are being pushed by the explosion.

summary: The specification asks you to explain that light from distant galaxies is red-shifted, that more distant galaxies show greater red-shift and move away faster, and that this and the cosmic microwave background radiation are evidence that the universe is expanding from a small, hot, dense start (the Big Bang). It matters because it is how we know the history of the universe and is a classic 'evidence for a scientific model' question.

terms.d: The change in the observed frequency and wavelength of a wave when the source and the observer are moving relative to each other.
The increase in the observed wavelength of light from a source moving away from the observer, so features in the spectrum move towards the red end.
The decrease in the observed wavelength of light from a source moving towards the observer.
A dark line in a spectrum at a wavelength where atoms in the source's atmosphere have absorbed light; the pattern identifies elements.
An instrument that splits light into its spectrum so that the wavelengths present can be measured.
A very large group of stars, gas and dust held together by gravity; our galaxy is the Milky Way.
The stretching of space itself, so that distant galaxies move further apart.
The model that the universe began from a very small, extremely hot and dense region about 13.8 billion years ago and has been expanding ever since.
Electromagnetic radiation in the microwave region that fills the universe and comes from all directions, left over from the early hot universe.
An older theory that the universe has no beginning and always looks the same, with matter created as it expands; it cannot explain the CMB.
The distance that light travels in a vacuum in one year.
The distance from one point on a wave to the same point on the next wave, for example crest to crest.
The number of waves passing a point each second, measured in hertz (Hz).
Observations or measurements that support or contradict a scientific model.
The small cluster of galaxies, including the Milky Way and Andromeda, that is held together by gravity.

worked.ans: The wavelength of light from distant galaxies is increased (red-shift). More distant galaxies have greater red-shift, so are moving away faster. This means space is expanding. Working backwards, all matter was once in a very small, hot, dense region, which is the Big Bang model.
worked.q: Explain how the red-shift of light from distant galaxies provides evidence for the Big Bang model. (4 marks)
steps: Mark 1: the light from distant galaxies has a longer wavelength than expected, so it is red-shifted.
Mark 2: the further away the galaxy, the greater the red-shift, so the faster it is moving away.
Mark 3: this shows that the universe, or space itself, is expanding.
Mark 4: if the universe is expanding, in the past everything was closer together, so it began from a very small, hot, dense region, the Big Bang.

worked.ans: Galaxy C is furthest (largest shift, 28 nm). It is 7 times further away than galaxy A.
worked.q: In a laboratory a hydrogen absorption line has a wavelength of 656 nm. The same line is observed in light from three galaxies at 660 nm (galaxy A), 668 nm (galaxy B) and 684 nm (galaxy C). Which galaxy is furthest away, and how many times further is it than galaxy A if distance is proportional to red-shift? (3 marks)
steps: Find each shift = observed wavelength - laboratory wavelength.
The greatest red-shift is galaxy C, so it is moving away fastest and is the furthest.
If distance is proportional to red-shift: 28 / 4 = 7.

worked.ans: The CMB is microwave radiation arriving from every direction in space. The Big Bang model says the early universe was very hot and dense and full of short-wavelength radiation. As the universe expanded, this radiation was stretched to longer wavelengths, so it is now microwaves. The model predicted this leftover radiation and it was found, which supports the model. Together with the red-shift of distant galaxies, this is strong evidence for the Big Bang, and the Steady State theory cannot explain it.
worked.q: Describe what is meant by cosmic microwave background radiation and explain why it is evidence for the Big Bang. (6 marks)
steps: Describe: CMB is electromagnetic radiation in the microwave region that comes from all directions in space.
Origin: the Big Bang model says the early universe was extremely hot and dense, so it was full of high-energy, short-wavelength radiation.
Stretching: as space expanded, the wavelength of the radiation was stretched, and it is now in the microwave region.
Evidence: the Big Bang model predicts this leftover radiation, and it was detected, matching the prediction.
Add red-shift: together with the red-shift of galaxies, two independent observations agree with the model.
Conclusion: other theories, such as the Steady State theory, cannot explain the CMB, so the Big Bang model is better supported.
